detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

sources.name: ERCOT
sources.scope: Large generators with a full interconnection study requested, from the monthly Generator Interconnection Status report for Texas. Includes projects from study through commissioning.

sources.name: NYISO
sources.scope: Projects in the New York interconnection queue as NYISO publishes them.

sources.name: MISO
sources.scope: Projects in the Midcontinent generator interconnection queue, all statuses as MISO publishes them.

sources.name: Southwest Power Pool
sources.scope: Generator interconnection requests across the south-central US, all statuses as SPP publishes them, withdrawn requests counted separately.

sources.name: CAISO
sources.scope: Active generator interconnection requests on the California ISO grid, from the public queue report. Completed and withdrawn projects are counted separately.

analysis.body:
The five grid operators represented here — ERCOT, NYISO, MISO, Southwest Power Pool, and CAISO — collectively show 8,364 interconnection requests totaling roughly 1.33 million MW of planned generation and storage waiting to connect to the grid as of September 4, 2026. These are projects seeking permission to plug in, not data centers themselves, and the queues span very different geographies and reporting rules, so the numbers cannot simply be added to produce a single national figure. ERCOT's Texas queue alone accounts for 438,086 MW across 1,778 requests, while CAISO's active California queue is far smaller at 71,682 MW across 265 requests, reflecting both the different sizes of the grids and the different ways each operator counts projects — CAISO, for instance, excludes completed and withdrawn projects separately, and SPP counts withdrawn requests apart from the rest.

What makes these queues relevant to readers focused on AI infrastructure is the composition of what is being requested. Storage — the battery capacity that smooths out renewable intermittency and increasingly serves as a dispatchable resource for around-the-clock loads like data centers — is prominent in every queue that tracks it: 159,820 MW in ERCOT, 68,429 MW in MISO, 52,913 MW in SPP, and 46,944 MW in CAISO. Natural gas, which provides the firm, always-on power that heavy compute workloads demand, shows meaningful queued capacity in Texas at 78,092 MW and in SPP at 47,386 MW, with smaller but still substantial volumes in MISO at 30,236 MW, NYISO at 27,879 MW, and CAISO at 916 MW. The growth in both storage and gas requests in AI-dense states is consistent with the load profiles of large data center campuses, even though the queue data does not identify end customers.

The EIA commercial electricity sales figures for June 2026 offer a complementary lens: Texas reported 15,754 GWh of commercial-sector sales that month at an average price of $8.66 per MWh, while Virginia — the globally significant data center corridor — reported 7,771 GWh at $10.99 per MWh, and California reported 10,025 GWh at the highest price in the group, $27.33 per MWh. These are commercial-class sales across all buyers, not a direct measurement of data center consumption, but the scale and pricing in Virginia and Texas in particular are consistent with the concentration of large hyperscale facilities known to operate there. The gap between Virginia's relatively modest price and California's steep one helps explain why developers continue to favor mid-Atlantic and Texas locations for new builds.

Watch for whether ERCOT's gas queue — already the largest single fuel-and-region combination in this dataset at 78,092 MW — continues to grow in next month's Generator Interconnection Status report, which would signal sustained developer confidence in Texas as the preferred location for firm-power-hungry AI data center expansion.
